newsitem.title: USA: Ad study sees growing importance of Internet market.
newsitem.headline: Ad study sees growing importance of Internet market.

text.p: A leading ad agency said Wednesday its new survey shows companies should advertise more on the Internet if they want to reach a key demographic group: affluent, well educated Baby Boomer and Generation X men.

The men in their 30s and 40s who make up the core of Internet users in the Americas need to be reached through the medium, according to the study by the New York-based Bates USA agency, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters.

Bates, part of Cordiant Plc of London, dubbed these avid technology consumers "techthusiasts." They snap up new gadgets and other technology innovations as soon as they're available, making hits out of products like videocassette recorders and compact disc players.
Some media experts believe the growing use of the Internet by this group is starting to have a measurable impact on other media, showing up in the form of weaker television ratings.

"In the U.S. and Canada, Internet usage is at least partly responsible for eroding techthusiasts' use of television," said Craig Gugel, Bates executive vice president for new media and interactive research, who headed the study.

Bates surveyed more than 2,000 adults in North America. They concentrated on the estimated 85 million technology enthusiasts throughout the Americas who comprise 20 percent of the adult population in the region.
-- Slighty more than 51 percent of the technology buffs were active on the Internet in the United States and Canada.
-- The Internet's penetration will continue to grow by 6 percent a year, reaching 92 percent by 2005.
-- The Internet will become more mainstream, branching out from the core user group.
-- Questions regarding commercial viability will be replaced by worries about "overcrowding and clutter" as key marketing concerns.
The technology enthusiasts' role is being closely examined as a way of forecasting how the population as a whole will take to the Internet and how the Internet will displace other media.

The Bates study noted that technology pioneers were among the heaviest readers of newspapers and magazines, although they are less avid television watchers. These enthusiasts said they like to get editorial products delivered on the Internet and they are heavy users of e-mail.

Taken together, those findings point to likely growing demand for Internet-based content, Bates said. Just as important, Gugel said, the study group was friendly toward the concept of advertising sponsorships on the World Wide Web, and respondents said they would be likely to click on ads to get more information.
Gugel said advertisers should take advantage of technology enthusiasts' interest by using the Internet more.

"Marketers should now consider allocating ad dollars for Internet dollars to begin compensating for the (audience losses) they are increasingly experiencing through use of conventional electronic media," Gugel said.

The survey results should give comfort to the scores of ventures still trying to turn a profit by creating ad-sponsored sites on the Net. The Bates study concluded that "advertising and ad-sponsored editorial (content) are certain to have relatively stable futures on the interactive services."
Marketers are attempting to learn more about the group because their technology-friendly attitude tends to influence others, partly because of "rampant fear of being left behind."
